subject: ela
description: Students produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience. They recognize when ideas are developed with enough relevant detail, when sentences and paragraphs are ordered logically so the writing flows, and when the word choice, tone, and formality match the assignment and the intended reader. They identify writing that is vague, disorganized, padded with off-topic detail, or mismatched in tone, and they choose revisions that make the writing clearer and more coherent. Because this is a writing standard, every item embeds the full prompt, sentence, paragraph, or short passage it depends on inside the item itself, so the student needs nothing external. Items test the components of clear and coherent writing through analysis, selection, and short revision rather than full multi-paragraph essays.
subSkills: Match the style, tone, and level of formality of a piece of writing to its task, purpose, and audience (for example, a letter to the principal versus a text to a friend)
Identify the task and purpose of a writing prompt (inform, explain, narrate, persuade) and recognize whether a draft fulfills it
Recognize when an idea is underdeveloped and choose the detail or example that develops it most clearly
Distinguish relevant supporting detail from off-topic or padding detail that weakens coherence
Order sentences within a paragraph in a logical sequence so ideas connect smoothly
Choose the best place to add a sentence, or the best transition, so a paragraph stays coherent
Identify a sentence that breaks the flow or unity of a paragraph and should be removed
Revise vague, wordy, or unclear wording into precise, clear language without changing the meaning
Keep tone and style consistent within a single piece of writing

problemArchetypes.name: Match style to audience
problemArchetypes.example: Read the prompt embedded in the item: 'Write a note asking your school principal for permission to start a chess club.' Which opening best fits this task, purpose, and audience? Options include a formal request ('Dear Principal Adams, I am writing to request permission to start a chess club.') and casual ones ('Hey, can we make a chess club? It would be so cool.'). Answer: the formal request, because the audience is a school authority and the purpose is a serious request.

problemArchetypes.name: Develop an underdeveloped idea
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence in the item: 'Our town should build a new library.' Which sentence best develops this idea with a clear, relevant detail? Options include 'A new library would give students a quiet place to study and free access to books.' versus 'Libraries are buildings.' Answer: the first, because it adds a specific, relevant reason that supports the idea.

problemArchetypes.name: Spot the off-topic sentence
problemArchetypes.example: Read the short paragraph embedded in the item about how to plant a garden. Three sentences explain the steps in order; one sentence says 'My favorite color is green.' Which sentence should be removed to keep the writing coherent? Answer: the favorite-color sentence, because it does not connect to the topic of planting a garden.

problemArchetypes.name: Order the sentences
problemArchetypes.example: Read the four scrambled sentences embedded in the item that describe a morning routine. Which order makes the paragraph clear and logical? Answer: the sequence that follows the natural time order (wake up, get dressed, eat breakfast, leave for school).

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the clearer revision
problemArchetypes.example: Read the wordy sentence in the item: 'The thing that happened was that the bus, which was the one we take, came late on account of the fact that there was traffic.' Which revision is clearest? Answer: 'Our bus came late because of traffic,' because it states the idea precisely without padding.

problemArchetypes.name: Place the added sentence or transition
problemArchetypes.example: Read the paragraph embedded in the item with a numbered blank between sentences. Which sentence or transition best fills the blank so the paragraph stays coherent? Answer: the choice that connects the idea before the blank to the idea after it.

problemArchetypes.name: Fix the inconsistent tone
problemArchetypes.example: Read the mostly formal paragraph in the item that contains one slangy sentence ('This data is super legit, no cap.'). Which revision keeps the tone consistent? Answer: 'This data is reliable and well documented,' because it matches the formal style of the rest of the paragraph.

Easy.description: A single sentence or a short two-sentence pair (roughly 10 to 25 words total) embedded in the item, with a clearly stated prompt, task, or audience. The task is identify-level: pick the sentence that fits the audience, choose the obviously clearer wording, name whether a tone is formal or casual, or spot a single off-topic sentence. Only one component of clear and coherent writing is tested and the correct answer is unmistakable.
constraints: Stimulus is one short sentence or a two-sentence pair included in the prompt
Tests exactly one component (audience match, single clear revision, one obvious off-topic detail)
Identify-level task: select or label, no construction required
Distractors are clearly weaker (an obviously wrong tone, a vague sentence, or an unrelated detail)

Medium.description: A short paragraph or a prompt plus a 3 to 5 line draft (roughly 30 to 60 words) embedded in the item. The task is analyze-level: choose the detail that best develops an idea, identify which of several sentences breaks the flow and should be cut, order a short set of sentences logically, or choose the revision that matches the task and audience. The student must weigh more than one option that is partly defensible.
constraints: Stimulus is a short paragraph or a prompt with a brief draft in the prompt
Tests development, organization, relevance, or style match
Analyze-level task: choose, order, or revise based on clarity and coherence
Distractors are plausible partial fits (a related but weaker detail, a nearly correct sentence order, a tone that is close but off)

Hard.description: A multi-sentence paragraph or two short related drafts (roughly 60 to 110 words) embedded in the item, sometimes containing a flaw to repair. The task is evaluate-level: judge which full revision best improves clarity and coherence across the paragraph, decide where an added sentence or transition belongs so the whole paragraph flows, determine why a draft fails to match its stated task and audience and what would fix it, or choose the version whose development, organization, and style are most appropriate to the assignment. Requires inference about the writer's purpose and how the parts of the writing fit together.
constraints: Stimulus is a 3 to 6 sentence paragraph or two short drafts included in the prompt
Tests how multiple components interact: development, organization, style, and audience together
Evaluate-level task: select the best full revision, placement, or version and judge it against task, purpose, and audience
Requires inference to judge logical flow, coherence, and whether the writing fits its purpose and reader

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student mismatches style to audience, treating casual or slangy language as acceptable for a formal task
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'Hey, can we make a chess club? It would be so cool' as the opening for a formal request to the principal instead of a respectful, formal version

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks more words or longer sentences always mean clearer or better writing, favoring padded wording over precise wording
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses the wordy, repetitive sentence as the clearest instead of the concise revision that states the idea directly

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats any sentence about the general topic as relevant, ignoring whether it actually develops the main idea
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Keeps an off-topic detail such as 'My favorite color is green' in a paragraph about planting a garden because it appears in the same paragraph

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student ignores logical or time order and arranges sentences by what sounds interesting first rather than by what makes the paragraph flow
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Orders a how-to or sequence paragraph out of step order so the result is confusing, instead of following the natural sequence

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses development with simply restating the idea, adding a sentence that repeats the point rather than supporting it with a relevant detail
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a circular restatement such as 'Libraries are buildings' to develop 'Our town should build a library' instead of a specific supporting reason

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student lets tone shift within a piece, accepting one casual or emotional sentence inside otherwise formal writing
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Keeps a slangy line such as 'This data is super legit, no cap' inside a formal paragraph instead of a matching formal revision

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student judges a draft only by whether its sentences are correct, not by whether it fits the assigned task, purpose, and audience
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks a grammatically fine but purpose-mismatched draft (a story when the prompt asked for an explanation) as the best response to the prompt
